en: Ruby stones as large as horses' heads,
All kinds of possessions mingled—
When he saw those things,
His poor soul was overcome.
When Manas took Beijing,
When he wreaked havoc on the Chinese,
Five carpets came as gifts;
Those famous possessions were here.
They appeared before his eyes.
‘Where is my father who won these?’
The orphan grieved still more,
And tears poured from his eyes.
His armguards looming broad,
The great carpet on which their khan sat;
With his berenji wrap girded on,
The great carpet on which their bey sat;
Of the Chinese wearing stone badges,
The great carpet where their purest sat;
Of the red-tasseled Chinese,
The great carpet where their mightiest stood;
Of the Manchus wearing jackets,
The great carpet where their strongest stood.
When valiant Manas lived,
When he ruled over Beijing,
The great carpet he received as a gift.
To Beijing, untrodden by the four caliphs,
When his strength could reach,
The great carpet he seized.
To Beijing, unreached by the Deluge,
When his host arrived,
The great carpet he took for use.
The wonder of that carpet:
Its weft was silk, its outer face gold—
Ah, a sight for human eyes to gaze upon!
Cast into water for forty years,
Its edges would neither warp nor fade;
Cast into water for eighty years,
It would neither fray nor rot.
The great carpet with golden patterns,
From my valiant father Manas,
The great carpet left as a gift.
My valiant mother Kanykei
Gathered its edges and stitched them,
Entrusting it to her hero Semetey.
She folded it again and packed it,
And entrusted it to her orphan.
Stretched out like a dead person,
With gold laid at its base,
My mother Kanykei, that troublesome one,
Left it as a trust.
When he saw his possessions,
The boy's heart was distracted.
Red gold coins, white gold—
The wealth looked wonderful.
There was wealth, there was property;
Indeed, everything eyes had ever seen was there.
When he looked at the threshold,
An object left by his father
Stood there in sight.
When he twisted and pulled it free,
Its face had been coated with poison,
Its haft inlaid with gold;
Every part was skillfully fitted.
Poor Bölökbai, the master craftsman, had made it.
None it struck remained alive;
When it met its mark, it never went in vain.
That was a treasure to take out,
The battle-axe left by his father, generous Manas,
That was a keen blade to carry.
He took the battle-axe as a gift:
A great companion if carried along,
Needed for the life entrusted to him.
Having seen the treasury, he sealed it.
Grateful to Allah,
Giving thanks to God,
The poor orphan prayed fervently
To his father, Lord Manas.
One might well give one's life
For a mother such as Kanykei.
“My mother, my towering plane tree,
I took this from the treasury,
A needed thing left by my father, Khan Manas.”
As the boy walked, his heart was distracted.
The battle-axe in his hand
Looked like his father Manas himself.
Taking the axe from the treasury,
Semetey turned back.
Angling along on Kökcholok,
Fierce Bakai led the way.
As Bakai traveled farther,
He spoke of another wonder:
“Oh, my spring that feeds a valley river,
Oh, my dear one, found when I was near death!
There are wonders in many places;
My orphan, my delight, know this.
I will take you where you have not gone,
Bring you in where you have not entered,
Make you sense what you have not sensed.
If your khan uncle Bakai does not die,
If he does not face the Last Judgment,
I know the roads in many places,
I know the peoples in many places.
My comfort left by Manas,
I know many wonders.
When fierce Manas was khan,
When great prosperity was ours,
Your uncle, Sultan Bakai's
Marten-fur hat upon his head—
Who has not worn it at a jaunty tilt,
When we traveled to many places,
When troops of many tribes marched,
When countless multitudes marched,
Falcon Manas was a lion.
At the foot of the banner beside Manas,
It was I, Bakai, who stood.
Since that Manas died,
Since I suffered such torment,
Into my mouth, too small for millet,
A yearling calf's head fitted well.
Into my mouth, too small for wheat,
A bull's head fitted perfectly.
My poor soul would not eat horse-belly fat;
Since bloodthirsty Manas died,
I have yearned for even plain water.
Parted from my leopard,
Grieving, crying ‘My bloodthirsty one!’
Parted from my twin,
I grieved for Manas,
And my dark eyes became mere specks.
Since my falcon Manas passed,
Leaving his uncle, upright Bakai,
Behind him as he went,
I was a gorge; I became a road.
I was a leopard; I was humbled.
My child, I was a sheltered nook; I became a road.
Parted from the one who eased my sorrow,
Thus, my child, I was brought low.
When Manas passed at Keng-Shor,
When he went to the other world,
When we camped along the river,
My foal, when it was as though a fire had died,
She sent to spacious Mecca.
Ak Eshen was in spacious Mecca;
She had Ak Eshen brought.
She sent to Andijan,
For Aikojo in his mottled robe,
And had Aikojo brought.
The forty eshens in Andijan,
She had them brought as well.
My dear child Kanykei,
Without letting a single soul know,
Sent riders back and forth.
A plan that no one knew,
My child devised and found.
Without a word to any person,
Without confiding in anyone,
At Echkiliktin Kara-Zoo,
That vast and silent mountain,
She had the black cliff face dug out,
And entrusted your father, Khan Manas, there.
She sent to Medina;
From Arabia, whose speech was unknown,
She had eighty strong men brought.
Ten of the eighty had died;
Seventy strong men arrived.
Your mother did not let this be known.
To those seventy strong men
She gave a thousand dark camels,
Gave mares in herds of a thousand,
Gave horses for them to ride,
Gave robes for them to wear.
‘People of true Mecca,’ she said,
Paying homage and giving her hand.
When the strong men thirsted,
She stirred kumis and gave them honey.
She broke off sugar like snow,
And cut chunks of yellow butter.
She gave tea in a metal ewer,
And served their meals at ease.
When the strong men wished to eat,
She gave plentiful tail fat and butter.
She gave keen iron crowbars,
Gave fine steel hoes as tools.
Each day, to the strong men,
She gave gold and jewels by the pood.
She had the black cliff face opened,
And Khan Manas's grave
She had dug out there.
Go inside, dear one, and you will see;
‘My mother was capable indeed,’
You will know it then.
Your poor mother in mourning—
God's sun in the sky grew clouded,
And sixty worries came at once to her head.
‘He had many claimants who disputed with him,
Many enemies who fought him with spears,
Many beys with evil intent,
Many peoples of a different grave.
I will not leave him in an open place,’ she said.
‘On the Day of Judgment, your father's
Black donkey I will not become.
Unless I hide my bloodthirsty one away,
I will fare ill in the other world.
If I bury him out in the open,
Yet see, there is distress within me.
While the generous one was alive,
The enemies who exchanged fire with him
Will open your grave,’ she said.
‘Dragging you onto the road,
They will bring such sorrow.
As though taking revenge upon the dead,
They will have full-grown dogs tear you apart.
Of those stubborn foes who fought him,
Thus they will take their great revenge,’ she said.
She devised a plan and settled her words,
Keeping her stratagem locked within.
Your mother dug; we buried him.
Your fierce, tempestuous mother's
Saintly wisdom we truly saw.
Now, Semetey, hear your story.
She prepared the proper rites,
And carried out her deeds,
Letting no one know
The secret mischief in her heart.
She mastered thought and found the words,
Devised each action firmly.
Could a woman be like this?
My child, a woman like Kanykei—
The person who called her merely female,
The soul who called her a mere woman—
Truly be called a man?
Screaming, weeping, grieving,
Parted from true Manas,
Her bloody face was torn,
Her black hair hung loose,
Upon her bulky dark head.
Parted from her bloodthirsty one,
At thirty-two years of age,
With you, a young boy, beneath her arm,
Her poor soul suffered humiliation.
When my Manas perished,
The elders Koshoi and Töshtük were there,
Those who had been close to Manas—
All his mighty men were there.
Gave six swift horses
To poor me, his uncle Bakai,
‘Let him come beside the dwelling,
Let him see a plan of mine,’ she said,
And gave a palm-sized letter.
The poor mourner felt shy,
And sent it with a lowly slave woman.
The slave woman came and gave the letter,
Without holding back, she gave it quickly.
When I read her letter,
It was written in Arabic.
